speaker_role: former admissions officer (Andrew Hoffman, former admissions officer at Vanderbilt and Swarthmore)
commercial_incentive: Yes - promotes his paid application review service for high school seniors, though the bulk of the video is detailed informational content
key_insights: The counselor-submitted 'school report' tells admissions two things: information about the student and, often overlooked, context about the high school itself (curriculum access, demographics, community type)

Counselors rate how demanding a student's curriculum is relative to classmates at the same school (options: less demanding, average, demanding, very demanding, most demanding), which the speaker says was one of the first things reviewed and could steer committee discussion

Admissions officers interpret AP/rigor counts relative to what's actually offered at that school (e.g., 6 APs at a school offering 8 vs. one offering 35 mean very different things), not as an absolute number
Schools report caps/limits on how many advanced courses students can take per year (e.g., some cap sophomores at one AP); officers use this to avoid penalizing students for school policy
Community service hours reported on a transcript are weighed differently depending on whether the school requires community service for graduation - mandatory hours carry less signal

Counselors also submit personal/character ratings (academic achievement, extracurricular accomplishment, personal qualities/character, overall); a high academic rating but only average personal qualities rating can raise concern in committee

A missing counselor letter (common at large public schools with high student-to-counselor ratios) is not treated as a red flag by admissions officers, who know which schools/counselors are resource-strapped

The school profile (separate from the school report) explains grading scale, curriculum structure, course access policies (open vs. restricted enrollment), and prior graduating class data - officers actively look for it after reading the transcript
Midyear grade reports (sent Jan/Feb) are compared against a student's existing transcript trend; committee looks for consistency or unexpected changes
Early Decision applications require the counselor to also sign the ED agreement form, confirming they've discussed the binding commitment with the student and family
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker states roughly a third of US high schools (or fewer, now) still report an official class rank
Speaker gives an example of Georgia high schools adding bonus points for AP/advanced courses, producing final grades like 104 or 107 that must be converted back (e.g., to a 97 or 94) by admissions
Speaker mentions some East African school systems where 84% nationally represents the top of the class, which could otherwise be misread as a 'B average' by an untrained reader
Speaker states midyear grade reports are typically submitted by end of January or mid-February
notable_or_distinctive: Provides an unusually detailed, insider walkthrough of the counselor-submitted documents (school report, counselor letter, school profile, transcript, international supplement, midyear/final reports, ED agreement) that most applicants never see, drawn from the speaker's direct experience reading these forms at Vanderbilt and Swarthmore.
reliability_notes: Speaker's credentials (former AO at two selective schools) lend credibility, but the video ends with a paid application-review pitch; specific institutional practices described (e.g., exact rating scales, internal shorthand like 'MDurick') reflect his particular past employers and may not generalize to all colleges.
